text: Every summer, volunteers wade into the rock pools at Hollowgum Point for the annual Sea Slug Count. Armed with buckets, magnifying glasses and waterproof notebooks, they spend a low tide searching under ledges and among the seaweed for nudibranchs, the brilliantly coloured sea slugs that live along the coast. Most years, the count is pleasant but unremarkable: volunteers record around thirty species, eat a sausage from the barbecue and go home. This year was different. Eleven-year-old Ruby Tan, attending for the first time, spotted a slug no longer than a grain of rice. It was electric purple with orange tips, and none of the experts recognised it. One of them was so surprised that she dropped her notebook in the pool. Photographs were sent to the state museum, where a marine biologist confirmed that the slug had never been described by science. Under the rules for naming animals, the scientist who formally describes a new species chooses its name, but she has invited Ruby to suggest one. Ruby is considering Grape Fizz. She admits she only came along because her grandmother made her, and she had planned to spend the day looking for crabs. Next year's count is expected to attract three times as many volunteers, and organisers have asked newcomers to tread carefully, because rock pools are fragile and the next undiscovered species could be underfoot.
